design_detail: Retrospective quantitative content analysis (the authors' term: retrospective observational study; not about drugs specifically). All 462 press releases on published biomedical or psychological studies with possible relevance to human health issued in 2011 by the 20 Russell Group universities (of 4093 press releases), their peer-reviewed journal articles, and 668 associated print or online UK national news stories found through Nexis, BBC, Reuters and Google (no broadcast news; 0 to 10 stories per press release). Each set was coded with a published protocol for three kinds of statement going beyond the journal article: advice to readers (four levels), causal claims from correlational (cross-sectional or longitudinal observational) results (a seven-point scale), and inference to humans from studies of animals, cells or simulations (three levels). Generalized estimating equations (exchangeable working correlation) gave percentages and odds ratios with news stories clustered within press releases; news uptake was compared between press releases with and without exaggeration (pp. 1–3; Fig 1, p. 7).
can_establish: How often, in health press releases of leading UK universities in 2011 and the national news based on them, advice, causal language and claims about humans were stronger than in the journal article, and how closely exaggeration in news went with exaggeration in the press release.
cannot_establish: That press releases caused the exaggeration in news (the design is correlational, as the authors say, p. 4); whether the stronger statements were scientifically unjustified (not judged, p. 4); how far the journal articles themselves overstate their data (the article is the baseline); or whether the same holds in other countries, years, broadcast media or for drug research in particular.

sample.recruitment: A census of documents: press releases from the public online repositories of the 20 Russell Group universities for 2011, their journal articles, and national print and online news found through Nexis, BBC, Reuters and Google (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Press releases based on published peer-reviewed studies with possible relevance to human health (biomedical and psychological sciences): 462 of 4093, the other 3631 being not health related or not based on a peer-reviewed article (Fig 1, p. 7). Broadcast news excluded (p. 2). Each analysis used the relevant subset: advice anywhere in article, press release or news (213 press releases); correlational studies (182); studies in animals, cells or simulations (105). Interventional, qualitative and simulation designs were not analysed for causal claims (pp. 2–3).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (documents). The universities are not named beyond 'Russell Group', and the topics and designs of the 462 studies are described only in the supplementary file (not read).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The news analyses include only press releases with at least one news story (116, 95 and 48 in the three analyses) (p. 3; Table, p. 6).
sample.selection_effects: One country, one year, 20 leading research universities, health-related press releases only; the authors expected no difference from other UK or international press releases but did not test it (p. 2). Journals' own press releases were not studied; some studies had both, which the authors say could only increase the share of news with an exaggerated press-release source (p. 4).

exposure.measurement: The 'exposure' is exaggeration in the press release relative to the journal article: the press release's title and first two sentences (causal claims) or whole text (advice), against the article's abstract and discussion; coded with a protocol available online, 27% of press releases and articles and 21% of news stories double coded (concordance 91%, mean κ = 0.88) (pp. 2–3).

comparison.controls: Press releases without exaggeration, and their news, against press releases with exaggeration, and their news, within each of the three analyses.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The analogue is features of the study or article (for example its news value) that could lead both press offices and journalists to stronger claims, which the authors name as alternative explanations (p. 4).

outcomes.instruments: Advice: four levels (none; implicit; explicit but not to the reader or general public; explicit to the reader or general public). Causal statements from correlational results: seven-point scale (no statement; explicit statement of no relation; correlational; ambiguous; conditional causal; can cause; unconditionally causal), stronger statements trumping weaker ones. Human inference from non-human studies: explicitly non-human, implicitly human, explicitly human. Caveats and justifications were also coded (pp. 2–3).
outcomes.validity_norms: The journal article is the baseline for what is justified; the authors did not judge whether stronger statements were scientifically warranted and argue that their exaggeration rates are probably underestimates because articles may already overstate (pp. 2–4).
outcomes.operationalization: Exaggeration: a statement in the press release or news stronger than any in the journal article's abstract and discussion (more direct advice, more deterministic causal wording, or a more human-directed inference). On the seven-point scale, 'associated with' counts as correlational and 'linked to' as ambiguous, one step stronger (pp. 2–3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported (three primary analyses, plus uptake comparisons and secondary analyses).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Each set (article, press release and news) was coded as a set, so news coding was not blind to the press release (p. 2).

analysis.effect_sizes: Exaggeration in press releases relative to the article: advice 40% (bootstrapped 95% CI 33% to 46%), causal claims 33% (26% to 40%), inference to humans 36% (28% to 46%) (p. 3). News overall: 36% (29% to 44%) with exaggerated advice, 39% (31% to 49%) with more deterministic causal statements than the article, 47% with inflated inference to humans (p. 3). News exaggeration when the press release was or was not exaggerated: advice 58% (48% to 68%) vs 17% (10% to 24%), difference 41% (28% to 53%), OR 6.5 (3.5 to 12.4); causal claims 81% (70% to 93%) vs 18% (9% to 27%), difference 63% (49% to 78%), OR 19.7 (7.6 to 51.4); human inference 86% (77% to 95%) vs 9.6% (0% to 19%), difference 76% (63% to 89%), OR 56.1 (14.9 to 211) (p. 3; Table, p. 6). News uptake (at least one story) with vs without exaggeration: advice 50/85 (59%) vs 66/128 (52%), 95% CI of the difference −6.4% to 21%; causal claims 34/60 (57%) vs 61/122 (50%), −9% to 22%; human inference 19/38 (50%) vs 29/67 (43%), −13% to 27%; odds ratios 1.3 (0.8 to 2.4), 1.3 (0.6 to 3.0) and 1.3 (0.7 to 2.5) (pp. 3–4; Table, p. 6). Stories per press release with vs without exaggeration: 3.4 vs 2.8 (advice), 2.7 vs 2.8 (causal claims), 2.5 vs 2.3 (human inference), every interval of the difference including zero (p. 4).
analysis.covariates: None; the generalized estimating equations adjust only for the clustering of news stories within press releases (p. 3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The coding protocol, all 462 coding sheets, data files and analysis programs are public (figshare, doi 10.6084/m9.figshare.903704); the paper does not say whether the protocol was registered before coding. The transparency statement says that any discrepancies from the study as planned have been explained (p. 5).
analysis.selective_reporting: The three primary analyses are reported with intervals; further analyses (secondary statements, caveats, justifications, the between-university correlation, quotes and study facts, a survey of scientists, news outlets) are summarized in the text and detailed in the supplementary file, which was not read (pp. 3–5).
analysis.power: Not reported. The human-inference news analysis rests on 48 press releases and 115 stories, hence its wide interval (OR 14.9 to 211).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A third or more of these press releases stated advice, causal claims or human relevance more strongly than the journal article; news based on an exaggerated press release usually carried the same exaggeration, news based on an accurate one seldom did; and press releases with exaggeration were not detectably more likely to be covered, though increases in coverage of up to about 21 to 27 percentage points are within the intervals.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes, carefully, that exaggeration in news is strongly associated with exaggeration in press releases (p. 1), and the authors state that the design does not show a causal relation (p. 4). The 'What this study adds' box and the discussion go a step further: most exaggeration in news was already present in press releases (p. 6), it did not arise anew in the media (p. 4), and most of the responsibility must lie with the scientific authors (p. 5). The first two are supported descriptively; the third rests on a cited earlier study and on a survey reported in the supplement, not on the content analysis. That exaggeration showed no evidence of increasing uptake (pp. 1, 4) is not evidence of no effect: all three point estimates favour more uptake (OR 1.3 each). The abstract describes the third analysis as inference from animal research, though it covered studies of animals, cells or simulations (pp. 1, 3).

timeline.event: Earlier study cited by the authors: of 200 randomly selected medical press releases from 2005, 29% were rated exaggerated and fewer than half gave appropriate caveats (Woloshin et al., 2009, as summarized on p. 2); not read

Earlier study cited: in 23 press releases and 71 news stories on cancer genetics, two thirds of press-release claims were at least as deterministic as the news (Brechman et al., 2009, as summarized on p. 2); not read

Spin in 72 reports of trials with non-significant primary outcomes: 58% of abstract conclusions presented the result more favourably than the data, the kind of overstatement in journal articles that the authors expect makes their own figures underestimates (p. 4)

Earlier study cited: in 70 trial press releases with their abstracts and 41 news stories, news contained spin absent from the abstract in only four cases (Yavchitz et al., 2012, as summarized on p. 2); not read

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no later replication was read for this card. The authors report ongoing work on journals' press releases (p. 4); the earlier, smaller studies they cite point the same way.

funding.funder: British Psychological Society, Experimental Psychology Society, Wales Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience, the Wellcome Trust, the Economic and Social Research Council, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, and Cardiff University (p. 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: ICMJE forms completed. The authors declare that the study was supported by the grants listed; no financial relationships with any organisations, except universities, that might have an interest in the submitted work in the previous three years; no financial relationships of spouses, partners or children that may be relevant; and no other relationships or activities that could appear to have influenced the submitted work (p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Cardiff University (psychology; journalism, media and cultural studies), Swansea University, and the Universities of New South Wales and Wollongong (p. 1). A professional advisory group included people from research councils, the Science Media Centre, BioMed Central, the BBC, The Guardian, The Sun and National Geographic (p. 5).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in which press releases on the same studies are issued with and without exaggeration (or with and without caveats), comparing the content and amount of the news that follows; and a repeat of the content analysis in other countries and years and for drug research, with news coded blind to the press release.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All health-related press releases on published studies in the 20 Russell Group universities' public repositories for 2011 (p. 2; Fig 1, p. 7); how far this stands for other institutions, countries or years is a question of indirectness, not of this item.
A census of eligible press releases (462 of 4093), with news found by systematic searches of databases and outlets (p. 2).
Press-release rates are estimated within about ±7 percentage points; the human-inference news analysis rests on 48 press releases (OR 14.9 to 211) (p. 3; Table, p. 6).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The selection and the three analysis subsets are described, but the universities, topics and designs of the studies are not given in the main text (supplementary file not read).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All relevant press releases enter the press-release rates; the news analyses cover all press releases with news, as designed (p. 3).

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Explicit, published coding scales; but 'exaggeration' means stronger than the journal article, not unjustified, and for causal claims the article's abstract and discussion are compared with only the title and first two sentences of press releases and news (pp. 2–3).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One protocol for all, with good agreement on double coding (91%, κ = 0.88, p. 2); but each article, press release and news set was coded as a set, so news coding was not blind to the press release, which could strengthen the press release–news association.
Generalized estimating equations for the clustering of stories within press releases, bootstrapped intervals, and null uptake results reported with intervals (pp. 3–4).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI items applied to a census of press releases and news, as the round brief asks for studies of how research is reported. The sample is complete for its frame and the coding scheme is explicit, published and reliable, so the prevalence figures are sound for UK university health press releases of 2011 judged against their journal articles. The limits are that exaggeration is measured against the article, not against the evidence; that news was coded together with its press release; and that the frame is one country and one year. The press release–news association is very strong but observational, and the uptake comparison could be confounded by news value, as the authors say. The source may be cited for how often press releases and news stated advice, causal claims and human relevance more strongly than the paper (a third to almost half), for how often a news story's exaggeration matched its press release, and for the finding that exaggeration was not detectably linked to more coverage. It may not be cited as proof that press releases cause exaggerated news, as a rate for drug news in particular, or as a measure of whether the stronger claims were wrong.

key_findings.finding: Of 462 health press releases from 20 leading UK universities in 2011, 40% (95% CI 33% to 46%) of the 213 with advice in the article, press release or news gave more direct or explicit advice than the journal article; 33% (26% to 40%) of the 182 on correlational results stated them more causally; and 36% (28% to 46%) of the 105 on studies in animals, cells or simulations inflated the relevance to humans.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Results › Exaggeration rates in press releases, 1st paragraph (p. 3)
key_findings.note: Denominators are the relevant subsets: 213, 182 and 105 press releases (pp. 2–3; Table, p. 6).

key_findings.finding: In the news, 36% (29% to 44%) of 360 stories gave more direct or explicit advice than the article, 39% (31% to 49%) of 261 stated correlational results more causally, and 47% of 115 inflated the inference to humans from non-human studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Association of news exaggeration with press release exaggeration, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 3); Table, story counts (p. 6)
key_findings.note: The 47% has no interval and cannot be reconciled with the conditional rates (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: When the press release was exaggerated, the news usually was too; when it was not, the news seldom was: advice 58% (48% to 68%) vs 17% (10% to 24%), OR 6.5 (3.5 to 12.4); causal claims 81% (70% to 93%) vs 18% (9% to 27%), OR 19.7 (7.6 to 51.4); inference to humans 86% (77% to 95%) vs 9.6% (0% to 19%), OR 56.1 (14.9 to 211).
key_findings.locator: Results › Association of news exaggeration with press release exaggeration, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 3); Table (p. 6); Fig 2 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: The 'What this study adds' box and the discussion state that most exaggeration in news was already present in the press releases; the discussion places most of the responsibility on the scientific authors, because press releases are drafted with scientists and approved by them (citing an earlier study and the authors' own survey).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Implications for practice, 1st paragraph (p. 5); What this study adds (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the story counts and conditional rates (p. 3; Table, p. 6), approximate because the percentages are model-based: about 76% of stories with exaggerated advice (about 100 of 132), 71% of those with exaggerated causal claims (about 75 of 105) and 86% of those with inflated human inference (about 40 of 47) followed an exaggerated press release.

key_findings.finding: Press releases with exaggeration were not detectably more likely to get news coverage: advice 59% (50 of 85) vs 52% (66 of 128); causal claims 57% (34 of 60) vs 50% (61 of 122); human inference 50% (19 of 38) vs 43% (29 of 67); OR 1.3 in each analysis (0.8 to 2.4; 0.6 to 3.0; 0.7 to 2.5). Nor did they get more stories per release (3.4 vs 2.8; 2.7 vs 2.8; 2.5 vs 2.3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effect of exaggeration in press releases on news uptake, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 3–4); Table (p. 6); Fig 3 (p. 8)
key_findings.note: The intervals of the differences (−6.4% to 21%, −9% to 22%, −13% to 27%) do not exclude increases of about 20 percentage points or more.

key_findings.finding: Caveats were rare in press releases; their presence or absence went with their presence or absence in the news, and caveats to causal claims were not linked to lower uptake (69% vs 51% with news; bootstrapped 95% CI of the difference −0.1% to 35%; small numbers).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effect of exaggeration in press releases on news uptake, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Between universities, the share of press releases with inflated statements ranged from 11% to 50% and the share with news coverage from 8% to 87%, without significant correlation (r = 0.13).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effect of exaggeration in press releases on news uptake, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the study is correlational and does not show that inflated press releases cause inflated news: if journalists did not read the press releases, features of the journal articles could still produce the association. They argue that converging evidence points to press releases as the main source of science news.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Caveats for our observational approach, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors did not judge whether stronger statements were scientifically justified, and argue that measured exaggeration is probably an underestimate because journal articles may already overstate or spin their findings.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exaggeration rates in press releases, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Discussion › Using journal articles as the baseline, 1st paragraph (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: The seven-point scale for statements about correlational results ranks 'associated with' as correlational, 'linked to' as ambiguous, 'might increase' as conditional causal, 'can increase' as can cause, and 'increases' as unconditionally causal; for press releases and news the title and first two sentences were coded, for journal articles the abstract and discussion.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Causal statements from correlational results, 1st paragraph (starts p. 2, ends p. 3)
key_findings.note: Bears on the use of 'linked to' as a marker of association: on this scale it is ambiguous, between correlational and causal wording.

key_findings.finding: The authors cite an estimate that fewer than 10% of non-human investigations ever succeed in being translated to human clinical use (ref. 24), as the reason why overselling animal results matters.
key_findings.note: A cited figure (van der Worp et al., 2010), not this study's data.

reporting_issues.issue: The overall share of news stories with inflated inference to humans (47%) is inconsistent with the two conditional rates and the story counts; editors' calculation: 86% of 47 stories and 9.6% of 68 give about 41%, while the other two overall rates (36% and 39%) agree with their conditional rates (about 37% and 40%). The 47% is the only overall news rate printed without an interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: For this analysis cite the conditional rates and the odds ratio, not the 47%.

reporting_issues.issue: The news-uptake sentence for inference to humans compares press releases without exaggeration with press releases 'with exaggerated advice', where exaggerated inference is meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Wording slip; the numbers (19 of 38) match the human-inference row of the Table (p. 6).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and its main outcome measures speak of inference to humans from animal research, while the analysis covered studies of animals, cells or simulations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 36% and the news figures refer to all non-human studies.

reporting_issues.issue: News coding was not blind to the press release: each article, press release and news set was coded as a set, and blinding is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The strength of the press release–news association may be inflated by coders' knowledge of the press release; the rates measured against the journal article are less affected.

reporting_issues.issue: Two statements in the discussion rest on a preliminary survey reported only in the supplementary file (section SI12, figure S2), which was not among the files: that press releases are approved by scientists, so that most responsibility lies with the scientific authors (a point that also cites an earlier study, ref. 20); and that a surprising number of scientists said their press releases were exaggerated. The quotes and study facts offered as converging evidence that press releases are the main source of science news are likewise only in the supplement (section SI11).
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements cannot be checked from the article; cite them as the authors' interpretation.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, BMJ 2014;349:g7015, published 9 December 2014), pages printed 'Page 1 of 8' to 'Page 8 of 8' and cited as pp. 1–8, all read; the Table (p. 6) and Figs 1–3 (pp. 7–8) checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; bar heights in Figs 2 and 3 not extracted beyond agreement with the printed percentages. The author-supplied supplementary file (sections SI1–SI13) and the figshare protocol and data were not among the files and were not read.
